summary: This document specifies the data formats and code points for the IS-IS extensions used by TRILL. TRILL provides optimal pair-wise forwarding without configuration in multi-hop networks with arbitrary topology, plus multipathing.

eli5.summary: TRILL switches share maps with a routing language called IS-IS. This defines exactly how those map messages are written.

subtitle: The exact IS-IS message formats and code points that let TRILL switches share maps, multicast listeners and capabilities.

tldr.problem: TRILL switches (RBridges) use the IS-IS routing protocol to learn about each other, but IS-IS has no standard way to carry TRILL-specific facts such as multicast listeners, VLAN duties, supported versions and distribution trees.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7176 defines two new IS-IS TLVs, a large family of sub-TLVs inside existing TLVs, two MTU-testing PDUs, and rules for how TRILL uses existing IS-IS PDUs and TLVs.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 6326 and adds multicast by IPv4 and IPv6 address, capability announcements, tree affinity, multi-topology support and fine-grained label support. The changes to existing TLVs are backward compatible.

today: RFC 7176 is a Proposed Standard and it obsoletes RFC 6326. The metadata for this RFC lists no later RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs IS-IS Extensions
sections.content:
TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links) forwards frames across multi-hop networks of any topology using a header with a hop count and link-state routing. The switches that run it are called Routing Bridges (RBridges) or TRILL Switches. They use IS-IS as the link-state protocol that tells each switch what the network looks like.

This document, together with RFC 6165, specifies the data formats and code points for the IS-IS extensions that support TRILL. The RFC notes that these formats and code points may also be used by technologies other than TRILL.

It obsoletes RFC 6326, which generally matched the base protocol in RFC 6325. The main additions are multicast group announcements by IPv4 and IPv6 address, capability announcements, a tree affinity sub-TLV, multi-topology support and control-plane support for fine-grained labels. Changes to TLVs and sub-TLVs from RFC 6326 are backward compatible.
sections.eli5: Imagine a club where everyone passes notes. This document is the rulebook for what goes on each note and where, so no one gets confused.

sections.title: The Group Address TLV
sections.content:
The Group Address (GADDR) TLV is IS-IS TLV type 142. It is carried in LSP PDUs and holds sub-TLVs that advertise multicast group listeners. The sub-TLVs under it form a new series of sub-TLV types.

There are six sub-TLVs, numbered 1 to 6. Three advertise listeners by VLAN (GMAC-ADDR for 6-byte MAC addresses, GIP-ADDR for 4-byte IPv4 addresses and GIPV6-ADDR for 16-byte IPv6 addresses). The other three, numbered 4 to 6, do the same with a 3-byte fine-grained label in place of the VLAN ID.

Each sub-TLV carries a topology ID (or zero if topologies are not in use), a VLAN ID or label (or zero if none is specified), a count of group records, and the records themselves. A record gives a number of sources and a group address followed by that many source addresses. A source count of zero means a listener for (*,G), that is, a listener not restricted by source. If the sources do not fit in one sub-TLV, the same group address may be repeated with different sources in another instance of the TLV.
sections.eli5: These notes say who wants to listen to which group broadcast. It is like a sign-up sheet for a radio channel, with a separate sheet for each kind of address.

sections.title: Port Capabilities in Hello Messages
sections.content:
Neighbouring switches exchange IS-IS Hello (IIH) PDUs. TRILL puts port-level information into these using sub-TLVs of the Multi-Topology-Aware Port Capability TLV from RFC 6165. There are five.

  • Special VLANs and Flags (sub-TLV 1) is carried in every IIH. It holds the port ID, a sender nickname (zero if the sender holds none), the outer VLAN, the Designated VLAN and the flag bits AF, AC, VM, BY and TR.
  • Enabled-VLANs (2) lists the VLANs enabled on the port as a bit-map starting at a given VLAN ID.
  • Appointed Forwarders (3) lets the Designated RBridge tell other switches on the link which VLAN ranges they forward, six bytes per appointment.
  • Port TRILL Version (7) gives the maximum TRILL version supported and 32 bits of capabilities and header flags. If it is missing, the sender is assumed to support only version zero and no optional capabilities.
  • VLANs Appointed (8) is a bit-map of the VLANs for which the sender believes it is Appointed Forwarder on that port.

VLAN ranges treat 0x000 and 0xFFF as invalid VLAN IDs, with specific rules: a range starting at 0x000 is read as starting at 0x001, one ending at 0xFFF is read as ending at 0xFFE, and a range whose end is less than its start is ignored.
sections.eli5: When two switches first meet, they swap name tags: which classrooms (VLANs) each one looks after, which rules they know, and what each of their ports is for.

sections.title: Capability Sub-TLVs in Link State PDUs
sections.content:
Information that the whole campus needs goes into link state PDUs (LSPs). TRILL carries it as sub-TLVs of the Router Capability TLV (type 242) and the MT-Capability TLV (type 144), using the same sub-TLV number in both. The sub-TLVs are:

  • TRILL-VER (13): maximum version and capability bits. If present it MUST occur in LSP number zero.
  • NICKNAME (6): nicknames the switch holds, with the priority to hold each and the priority to be a tree root.
  • TREES (7), TREE-RT-IDs (8) and TREE-USE-IDs (9): how many distribution trees to compute, which roots they have and which trees the sender wishes to use.
  • INT-VLAN (10) and INT-LABEL (15): the VLANs or fine-grained labels the switch is interested in, with multicast router attachment flags, an Appointed Forwarder status lost counter and a list of spanning tree root bridge IDs.
  • VLAN-GROUP (14) and LABEL-GROUP (18): VLANs or labels that share MAC address learning at the switch.
  • RBCHANNELS (16): which RBridge Channel protocols the switch supports, as byte-aligned bit vectors.
  • AFFINITY (17): a request that all switches connect a named switch as a child of the sender when computing the listed trees.

For multi-topology switches, capabilities announced for the base topology apply to every topology that has no separate announcement.
sections.eli5: Some news is for the whole school, not just your desk neighbour. These notes go on the school bulletin board: who is in charge of which hallway, and which shortcuts everyone should use.

sections.title: MTU Testing, Neighbors and Existing PDUs
sections.content:
The MTU sub-TLV (type 28) is carried in the Extended Reachability (22) and MT-ISN (222) TLVs. Its F bit is one if MTU testing failed at the required campus-wide MTU. The MTU field holds the largest successfully tested size for the link, or zero if untested.

The TRILL Neighbor TLV (type 145) replaces the standard IS Neighbor TLV in TRILL IIH PDUs on broadcast links. It lists neighbors by MAC address (SNPA) with a per-neighbor MTU and flags. The S and L flags show whether the list includes the smallest and largest MAC address. An IS that believes it has no neighbors MUST send the TLV with an empty list.

Two PDU types, the MTU-probe and MTU-ack, optionally measure the MTU on a link. Their TLV area MUST be padded with the Padding TLV to the exact size being tested.

For the rest, TRILL reuses existing IS-IS items. The area address is fixed at zero. A Protocols Supported TLV (129) with NLPID 0xC0 appears in TRILL IIH PDUs and LSP number zero. LSP number zero MUST NOT be originated larger than 1470 bytes, though a larger one received MUST be processed. The originatingLSPBufferSize TLV (14) MUST be in LSP number zero.
sections.eli5: Switches also check how big a package a road can carry, and they keep a list of the neighbours they can see. If a road cannot carry the big package, they write that down.

sections.title: Code Points and Registries
sections.content:
The RFC registers two IS-IS TLV types, the Group Address TLV (142) and the TRILL Neighbor TLV (145). It also assigns or carries over sub-TLV numbers under five existing TLVs and notes how many times each may occur in a PDU. IANA replaced RFC 6326 references in the registries with references to this document. For the sub-TLVs from NICKNAME through VLAN-GROUP, which previously existed only under TLV 242, the same numbers were added under TLV 144.

Reserved bits and capability bits are allocated by IETF Review. Two capability-flag sub-registries cover the TRILL-VER and PORT-TRILL-VER sub-TLVs, for example bit 0 of TRILL-VER for Affinity sub-TLV support and bit 0 of PORT-TRILL-VER for Hello reduction support. A third sub-registry, with Standards Action, covers TRILL Neighbor record flags: bit 0 for a failed MTU test and bit 1 for offering OOMF service.
sections.eli5: Every kind of note gets a number in an official phone book, so no two notes ever share the same number.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it raises no new security issues for IS-IS. General TRILL security considerations are in RFC 6325, and IS-IS security (RFC 5304 and RFC 5310) may be used to protect the messages described here.

It also warns that even with IS-IS authentication, replays of Hello packets can create denial-of-service conditions. These issues are similar in scope to those in Section 6.2 of RFC 6325, and the same mitigations may apply.
sections.eli5: Locks on the notes help, but someone can still copy an old note and hand it in again to cause trouble. The same fixes as before still work.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 6326
sections.content:
The RFC lists seventeen non-editorial changes. Notable ones: five new sub-TLVs under Group Address for IPv4, IPv6 and fine-grained-labeled addresses; the Port TRILL Version and VLANs Appointed sub-TLVs; the Interested Labels, RBridge Channel Protocols, Affinity and Label Group sub-TLVs; and multi-topology support.

The TRILL-VER sub-TLV gained four bytes of extended flags and capabilities and is now required in LSP number zero. The RFC argues this is backward compatible because RFC 6326 implementations supported only version zero with no optional capabilities, which is also what a missing sub-TLV means. Other changes allow a variable SNPA size in the TRILL Neighbor TLV (6 bytes is encoded as zero), make MTU PDU source ID sizes follow the IS-IS ID Length, and cap LSP number zero at 1470 bytes on origination.
sections.eli5: This is the list of what changed since the last rulebook. New kinds of notes were added, and the old notes still work.

items.desc: Numbers of trees to compute and use.
